```{r load}
# data from data-raw/vignette_method.R
vd <- function(f) system.file("vignette-data", f, package = "knowledge", mustWork = TRUE)
x <- readRDS(vd("method.rds"))
pipe <- x$pipeline
reg <- x$settings
fun <- x$funnel
fsp <- x$funnel_species
ex <- x$examples
pk <- x$picks
gs <- x$gradient_sensitivity
sg <- x$segment_at_site
n0 <- function(v) format(round(v), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
about <- function(v) format(signif(v, 2), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
pc <- function(v) paste0(round(100 * v), " %")
fn <- function(stage) fun$n[fun$stage == stage]
val <- function(key) gsub(";", ", ", reg$value[reg$key == key], fixed = TRUE)
issue <- function(n) {
  ifelse(is.na(n) | !nzchar(n), "",
         sprintf("[#%s](https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/knowledge/issues/%s)", n, n))
}
species <- c(BT = "bull trout", CH = "chinook", CO = "coho", GR = "grayling", RB = "rainbow trout", ST = "steelhead")
key_words <- function(k) {
  sp <- species[[sub("_.*$", "", k)]]
  paste(sp, if (grepl("_rear$", k)) "rearing" else "spawning")
}
# a rule string (size|gradient|near-river) in words
rule_words <- function(r) {
  p <- strsplit(r, "|", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  size <- if (grepl("^mad>=", p[1])) {
    sprintf("carries at least %s m³/s", sub("^mad>=", "", p[1]))
  } else {
    sprintf("is at least %s m wide", sub("^width>=", "", p[1]))
  }
  slope <- sprintf("no steeper than %s %%", round(100 * as.numeric(sub("^g<=", "", p[2])), 1))
  near <- if (p[3] == "none") "" else {
    q <- sub("^Q([0-9.]+)@D.*$", "\\1", p[3])
    d <- as.numeric(sub("^.*@D", "", p[3]))
    sprintf("; a smaller stream also counts if it passes the slope test and a river carrying at least %s m³/s lies within %s downstream",
            q, if (d >= 1000) paste(d / 1000, "km") else paste(d, "m"))
  }
  paste0(size, ", ", slope, near)
}
# an SVG Graphviz wrote, inline and no wider than the column (printed by a results = "asis" chunk)
svg_inline <- function(s) {
  s <- sub("^[^<]*(<\\?xml[^>]*>)?\\s*(<!DOCTYPE[^>]*>)?\\s*", "", s)
  cat(sub("<svg ", '<svg style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ', s, fixed = TRUE), "\n")
}
esc <- function(v) gsub(">", "&gt;", gsub("<", "&lt;", gsub("&", "&amp;", v, fixed = TRUE), fixed = TRUE), fixed = TRUE)
ch <- pk[pk$key == "CH_rear", ]
eras <- as.numeric(strsplit(reg$value[reg$key == "era_breaks"], ";", fixed = TRUE)[[1]])
st <- x$stability[x$stability$species_code == "CH" & x$stability$stage == "rear", ]
st[] <- lapply(st, function(v) if (all(grepl("^-?[0-9.]+$", v))) as.numeric(v) else v)
# step 8's words: the exact rule returns on most other splits but seldom on a redraw, it always stays a close call, and
# the choosing beats link's rule
stopifnot(nrow(st) == 1, st$seeds_same_rec > st$seeds_n / 2, st$seeds_rec_in_region == st$seeds_n,
          st$boot_rec_share < 0.5, st$honest_dev_rec < st$honest_dev_default,
          # step 2's words: most of the visits dropped at placement are too far from a stream (none within 500 m, or
          # past the snap limits)
          fn("with a usable point") - fn("far_snap") > (fn("FDIS visits") - fn("ws50_mismatch")) / 2)
lost_all <- fn("FDIS visits") - fn("no_link_segment")
lost_place <- fn("FDIS visits") - fn("ws50_mismatch")
stopifnot(fun$n[1] == 51587, nrow(ch) == 1, all(diff(fun$n) <= 0), lost_place / lost_all > 0.5)
# step 3's and the limits' words: most sites with fish start a segment of their own, more often than sites without,
# and sit on shorter segments; most picks are still close calls on the Atlas line's slope. A bundle without the two
# tables would make every comparison logical(0), which stopifnot() passes
stopifnot(!is.null(sg), !is.null(gs), nrow(gs) > 0, sg$at_site_fish > 0.5, sg$at_site_fish > sg$at_site_zero,
          sg$len_fish < sg$len_zero, sum(gs$pick_in_atlas_region) > nrow(gs) / 2)
```

The R package [`link`](https://newgraphenvironment.github.io/link/) maps where each fish species can live in British
Columbia's streams. For every stretch of stream it asks a few plain questions: is it big enough, is it too steep, and
can fish get to it? Each question has a cut-off. This article describes how we are testing those cut-offs against
evidence: the places crews have electrofished, and whether they caught the species there. We try many possible
cut-offs and keep the ones that best tell the two kinds of site apart, then check that they hold on parts of the
province they were not chosen from. The steps run in order, from the fish records to values link can read.

## What is a threshold, and what does "tuned" mean? {#thresholds}

A **threshold** is one of those cut-offs: a minimum stream size or a maximum slope. A **rule** is the few thresholds a
species uses together. A **tuned** threshold is one chosen by the test this article describes rather than taken from
the literature or set by judgment.

For chinook rearing, for example, link's current rule counts a stream as habitat if it `r rule_words(ch$default)`.
The fish records support a rule where it `r rule_words(ch$pick)`. We tested between
`r about(min(pk$rules))` and `r about(max(pk$rules))` candidate rules for each of the `r nrow(pk)` species and life
stages with enough records. The [chinook rearing article](chinook_rearing.html) works through one of them in full.

## What happens, in order? {#steps}

The `r nrow(pipe)` steps are each done by one package. Each box links to its package or source; each step links to its section
below.

```{r flow, results = "asis"}
svg_inline(x$svg$flow)
```

```{r step-detail}
# the code and settings of a step, folded under its text
detail <- function(step) {
  p <- pipe[pipe$step == step, ]
  fns <- strsplit(p$functions, ";", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  code <- vapply(fns, function(f) {
    if (grepl("^fwapg::", f)) {
      sprintf("<a href=\"https://smnorris.github.io/fwapg/03_functions.html#fwa-indexpoint\"><code>%s</code></a>",
              sub("^fwapg::", "", f))
    } else {
      sprintf("<code>%s()</code>", sub("^knowledge::", "", f))
    }
  }, "")
  s <- reg[reg$step == step, ]
  set <- if (nrow(s)) {
    paste0("<li>", esc(s$label), ": ", esc(gsub(";", ", ", s$value)), ifelse(nzchar(s$unit), paste0(" ", s$unit), ""),
           "</li>", collapse = "")
  } else ""
  open <- if (!is.na(p$issue) && nzchar(p$issue)) {
    sprintf("<li>Open work: <a href=\"https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/knowledge/issues/%s\">#%s</a></li>",
            p$issue, p$issue)
  } else ""
  paste0("<details><summary>Code and settings</summary><ul>",
         "<li>Run by: ", esc(gsub(";", ", ", p$scripts)), "; ", paste(code, collapse = ", "), "</li>",
         "<li>In: ", esc(p$inputs), ". Out: ", esc(p$outputs), "</li>", set, open, "</ul></details>")
}
```

### 1. `r pipe$label[1]` {#step-1}

The Province's electrofishing records [@provinceofbritishcolumbia2022FisheriesData]: where crews fished, how much
stream they covered, and what they caught. About `r about(fn("FDIS visits"))` site visits. A survey loaded twice is
kept once.

`r detail(1)`

### 2. `r pipe$label[2]` {#step-2}

Each site's map point is moved onto a stream of the BC Freshwater Atlas [@flnrord2021FreshwaterAtlasb], held in a
database by `fwapg` [@norris2024smnorrisfwapg]. Where the record names the site's tributary in a form the Atlas can
check, the site goes to the nearest stream of that tributary, even past a nearer stream, if it lies within
`r val("snap_limit_code")` m. Otherwise it goes to the nearest stream, if that lies within `r val("snap_limit")` m
([how a site is placed](#snap)). About `r about(fn("FDIS visits") - fn("ws50_mismatch"))` visits are dropped here,
most because the stream is too far away.

`r detail(2)`

### 3. `r pipe$label[3]` {#step-3}

link [@irvine2026linkDevelop] cuts the Atlas streams into short segments and records, for each species, whether fish
can reach each one and what link's current rules call habitat. It also cuts streams where the species it models have
been observed, using
`bcfishobs` [@norris2024smnorrisbcfishobs], so those observations shape the segments, but they never score a rule: they say where
fish were seen, not where they were looked for and missed. A catch of a species link models can be one of those
observations, so most stream-line sites that caught fish start a segment of their own.

`r detail(3)`

### 4. `r pipe$label[4]` {#step-4}

Flows come from `wet` [@irvine2026wetStream]. Mostly that is PCIC's modelled streamflow
[@schnorbus2018VICGlacierVICGL; @craig_etal2020Flexiblewatershed], carried onto Atlas streams by New Graph's fork of
`fwapg` [@norris_irvine2026NewGraphEnvironmentfwapg]. Where PCIC's flow does not reach a stream, or carries under a
fifth of wet's estimate on a stream's own line, it is wet's own water balance, fitted to Water Survey of Canada gauges
[@environmentandclimatechangecanada2021NationalWater]. About
`r pc(x$steps[["5"]][["routed"]] / x$steps[["5"]][["kept"]])` of the kept sites use PCIC's flow.

`r detail(4)`

### 5. `r pipe$label[5]` {#step-5}

Each kept site takes its segment's flow, width, access and slope, and the distance downstream to rivers of each size.
The slope is the segment's own, the slope link applies a rule to, not that of the whole Atlas line the segment was cut
from: a line can be gentle at one end and steep at the other, and averaging it would score a rule on a slope link
never tests.
Sites with no usable date, no fished area or time, no known catch, or no segment at their place drop out. About `r about(fn("no_link_segment"))` sites
remain.

`r detail(5)`

### 6. `r pipe$label[6]` {#step-6}

For each species we build thousands of rules around link's current values: different minimum stream sizes, slope
limits, and an allowance for small streams close to a big river.

`r detail(6)`

### 7. `r pipe$label[7]` {#step-7}

Each rule is scored and chosen as [described below](#se), where a table gives each species' choice. The model also accounts for how much stream was fished, which data set the record comes
from, its period (`r eras[1]` or earlier, `r eras[1] + 1` to `r eras[2]`, or later) and its watershed group, so a rule is not credited for those. A short trial run checks
the scoring before the full run starts.

`r detail(7)`

### 8. `r pipe$label[8]` {#step-8}

Many rules score almost alike, so the winner could come down to chance. We choose again three ways: with the groups
split `r st$seeds_n` other ways; leaving out one part of the groups, choosing on the rest and scoring the choice on the
part left out, for each part in turn; and on `r val("n_boot")` random redraws of the groups. For chinook rearing the
exact rule came back on `r st$seeds_same_rec` of the `r st$seeds_n` other splits but in only `r pc(st$boot_rec_share)`
of the redraws. It stayed a close call on all `r st$seeds_rec_in_region` splits, and choosing this way scored better than
link's rule on the parts left out (`r n0(st$honest_dev_rec)` against `r n0(st$honest_dev_default)`; lower is
better).

`r detail(8)`

### 9. `r pipe$label[9]` {#step-9}

We fit a smooth curve of how often the species is caught against stream size, distance to the river and slope, and
use it to grade every segment from low to high expected use. A species whose curve predicts no better than no rule at
all gets no grade.

`r detail(9)`

### 10. `r pipe$label[10]` {#step-10}

link's current rule and the chosen rule both go through the steps link itself uses, run by `fresh`
[@irvine2026freshFreshwater]: the rule's test, link's hand-entered habitat, and dropping rearing that has no spawning
nearby. On the Bulkley, those last two steps removed `r n0(ex$stages$dropped_default)` of the
`r n0(ex$stages$pre_default)` segments link's rule passed, so we compare whole runs, not the test alone.

`r detail(10)`

### 11. `r pipe$label[11]` {#step-11}

The chosen values are written under link's own parameter names, with the grades, so link can read them.

`r detail(11)`

## How is a site placed? {#snap}

A site's point is matched with every mapped Atlas stream within `r val("snap_search")` m, except the lines that carry
a stream across a watershed group's boundary (edge type `r val("snap_edges_excluded")`). Where the site's record names its
tributary, the nearest stream of that tributary is taken, kept if it lies within `r val("snap_limit_code")` m, even
when another stream is nearer. Otherwise the nearest stream is taken, kept if it lies within `r val("snap_limit")` m.
The table shows three sites: one kept on its nearest stream, one moved past a nearer stream to the tributary its record
names, and one dropped for its distance.

```{r snap}
row_of <- function(e, fate) {
  nb <- e$near
  data.frame(site = e$site$site_visit, fate = fate, stream = nb$blue_line_key,
             name = ifelse(is.na(nb$gnis_name), "(unnamed)", nb$gnis_name), distance_m = nb$distance_m,
             chosen = ifelse(nb$blue_line_key == e$site$blue_line_key, "yes", ""))
}
knitr::kable(rbind(row_of(ex$kept, "kept"), row_of(ex$moved, "moved"), row_of(ex$far, "dropped")),
             col.names = c("site visit", "fate", "Atlas stream", "name", "distance (m)", "snapped to"),
             caption = sprintf("Three %s sites and every Atlas stream within %s m of each.", ex$wsg, val("snap_search")),
             align = "llrlrl", row.names = FALSE)
```

## How are two rules told apart? {#se}

Each rule gets a **score**: how well "habitat or not" predicts where the species was caught, at sites in watershed
groups that were left out while the model was fitted. Lower is better.

Scores move with the sites we happen to have. The **standard error (SE)** of the difference between two rules' scores
says how far that difference would move with a different set of watershed groups. Rules whose scores are within
`r val("se_region")` SE of the best are **close calls**: the records cannot rank them. From the close calls we take
the one that changes link's current rule least.

One SE is a rule of thumb, fixed before the run. `r val("se_strict")` SE is the stricter reading, about the width of a
95 % interval: more rules become close calls, and the choice can stay nearer link's rule. Both are reported.

```{r picks}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `species and stage` = vapply(pk$key, key_words, ""),
  `link's rule` = vapply(pk$default, rule_words, ""),
  `close calls at 1 SE` = n0(pk$close_calls),
  `chosen at 1 SE` = vapply(pk$pick, rule_words, ""),
  `close calls at 1.96 SE` = n0(pk$close_calls_strict),
  `chosen at 1.96 SE` = vapply(pk$pick_strict, rule_words, ""),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "link's current rule and the rule chosen at each width of close call, for each species and stage tuned.",
  row.names = FALSE)
```

## Where are fish sampling records lost? {#lost}

Most of the records lost are lost when sites are put on the map (`r pc(lost_place / lost_all)` of the
`r about(lost_all)` dropped). A site far from any stream, or on the wrong tributary, cannot be trusted to sit on the
stream that was fished.

```{r funnel, fig.height = 3, out.width = "100%", fig.cap = "Site visits each step drops, in the order the steps run."}
f <- fun
f$drop <- c(NA, -diff(f$n))
f <- f[-1, ]
f$label <- factor(f$reason, levels = rev(f$reason))
ggplot(f, aes(x = drop, y = label)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0072B2", width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n0(drop)), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 60, size = 3.2, colour = "#333333") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(v) format(v, big.mark = ","), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(x = "site visits dropped", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

Each species then keeps the sites its rules can speak to: on a stream line (not in a river polygon, a wetland of
`r val("wetland_ha_min")` ha or more or a lake of `r val("lake_ha_min")` ha or more), of a usual fished area, where
link expects the species, with no code that could hide it and no natural barrier to it downstream. The score uses the
groups where the species was caught at some sites and not others.

```{r funnel-species}
w <- stats::reshape(as.data.frame(fsp[, c("species_code", "stage", "n")]), idvar = "species_code",
                    timevar = "stage", direction = "wide")
names(w) <- sub("^n\\.", "", names(w))
gb <- unique(fsp[, c("species_code", "groups_both")])
w$groups <- gb$groups_both[match(w$species_code, gb$species_code)]
w$species_code <- species[w$species_code]
w[-1] <- lapply(w[-1], n0)
knitr::kable(w[, c("species_code", "kept", "stream_branch", "fished_area", "in_range", "not_blocked", "no_barrier",
                   "scored", "groups")],
             col.names = c("species", "kept", "stream line", "fished area", "where expected", "not hidden",
                           "no barrier", "scored", "groups scored"),
             caption = "Rearing site visits per species after each filter.",
             align = "lrrrrrrrr", row.names = FALSE)
```

## Limits {#limits}

- A site's tributary code can name several Atlas streams, and the site goes to the nearest of them, which need not be
  the one the crew fished (`r issue("91")`).
- link's segments are shortest where fish were caught: `r pc(sg$at_site_fish)` of stream-line sites that caught fish
  start a segment of their own, against `r pc(sg$at_site_zero)` of those that caught none, and the median segment is
  `r n0(sg$len_fish)` m long against `r n0(sg$len_zero)` m. So which stretch a site's slope is worked out over depends
  on what the crew caught. Scored on the whole Atlas line's
  slope instead, the chosen rule is still a close call for `r sum(gs$pick_in_atlas_region)` of the `r nrow(gs)`
  species and stages (`r issue("92")`); slopes over a fixed length would not depend on where fish were caught
  (`r issue("70")`).
- Flows are 30-year averages, so no single dry year is in them.

## Which numbers shape the result, and which have been tested? {#settings}

Every number below shapes a result. Each was checked against the code and the run when this article's data were
written. **Source** says where the value came from: a published source, a convention set here, a value inherited
from link or bcfishpass [@norris2024smnorrisbcfishpass], or a value measured from data. **Tested** says whether the
result has been compared with another value. The untested rows come first: they are the work still to do.

Of the `r nrow(reg)` settings, `r sum(reg$tested == "yes")` have been tested and `r sum(reg$tested == "no" & reg$source == "inherited")`
of the untested ones were inherited.

<details><summary>All `r nrow(reg)` settings</summary>

```{r register}
r <- reg[order(reg$tested != "no", reg$source != "inherited", reg$step), ]
knitr::kable(data.frame(setting = r$label, value = gsub(";", ", ", r$value), unit = r$unit, step = r$step,
                        source = r$source, tested = r$tested, issue = issue(r$issue)),
             caption = "The settings, from inst/method/settings.csv.", align = "llllllr", row.names = FALSE)
```

</details>

## Software and citation {#software}

The steps run on the PostgreSQL tools [`fwapg`](https://smnorris.github.io/fwapg/) and New Graph's
[fork](https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/fwapg) of it, and on the R packages
[`link`](https://newgraphenvironment.github.io/link/) (segments, access and habitat),
[`wet`](https://newgraphenvironment.github.io/wet/) (flows), [`fresh`](https://newgraphenvironment.github.io/fresh/)
(the habitat tests) and [`knowledge`](https://newgraphenvironment.github.io/knowledge/) (the evidence and the
tuning). This article's data were written on `r x$meta$written` at commit `r x$meta$commit`. To cite this package:

```{r citation, results = "asis"}
cat(format(utils::citation("knowledge"), style = "text"), sep = "\n\n")
```
